I'm glad there's some other English reviews for this so far, but to contribute I'll go over some of the parts I don't think were covered:

Translation:
It's clear that this was a game meant for Chinese audiences, but the translation is serviceable. It has a bit of that jank that makes your head hurt a little bit if you read too much of it (mainly in the visual novel parts) but it's generally good enough to understand what's going on or what the intention was. I've definitely played worse. Some things are labeled weirdly, there's misspells and typos, but honestly it is good enough to enjoy the visual novel and use the UI just fine so it's not bad.

When I say it's clearly meant for Chinese audiences, some lines don't make any sense in English without the context that the original version is Chinese (for example characters saying Chinese proverbs in English, the wordplay doesn't work) but it's to be expected since sometimes jokes and things like that just don't translate well. You shouldn't have any real problems with this translation but it certainly isn't perfect.

Mechanics:
I thought the descriptions of the gameplay mechanics wasn't the clearest from reviews/the description so here's everything I've unlocked so far:
-Days
Each day you have a certain number of ap which essentially acts as your 'moves', and they recharge each time (once in the morning and once in the evening) and you start with 1 ap. Things like upgrading rooms, gathering materials, and bringing in new guests cost ap, but not everything does.
-Sanity and Oracles
Oracles are basically modifier cards you can get, like in a rougelike with cards. You get at least one opportunity to get one each part of the day and sometimes you can get multiple, but this costs your sanity. I believe losing all your sanity is game over, and you can choose to rest if you have ap to regain around 6 sanity (oracles seem to cost 1-6 sanity). Oracles can do things like boost guests you get, money earned, even clean your hotel. At the end of each month a blood moon occurs and consumes all your oracles, but if you have more than 10 you can choose a supreme oracle which is permanent.
-Alchemy
Alchemy works like the periodic table, each item has a value and you can fuse them together to get a new item with the value of the items added together. If you get a specific item you can level up your alchemy level (I think it boosts your chances to get rarer items but I'm not 100% sure). You can then also use alchemy items to bring in a bunch of guests to your hotel. You can get alchemy items from guests for free or you can buy them.
-Building your hotel
You can upgrade rooms in your hotel, usually for money and some materials you get from cleaning (cleaning requires ap). Usually it just boosts some stats but it also changes the appearance of the room which is really cute.
-Tasks
You get main tasks and side tasks, I believe if you fail main tasks you get a game over but I haven't failed any yet. They're generally related to earning enough, performing a certain action, or upgrading your rooms.

There's other mechanics too but I think those are the main ones (that I've gotten so far anyways). The game has a fun mix of chill idle style management and some legitimate strategy.

Plot:
A basic summary of the plot is that you are the adopted heir of a mysterious professor who died? Disappeared? I'm not sure and I don't remember but the bottom line is he's gone, and you receive his stuff (including the yard/hotel and a mysterious 'biodroid'). It's clear he was involved in some shady stuff and hosted auctions for rich nonhuman creatures who are all quite powerful. Some of them tried to have you killed so you couldn't claim your inheritance but that instead ended up in you basically becoming a werecat (yes every night you turn into a little one eyed cat). So far I really like the spooky vibe and characterization, and the story is definitely kind of out there which fits the aesthetic, so it goes along with the gameplay pretty well. The prologue is pretty long though, I think it took me almost an hour to get through. It's worth it but you can just fast forward if you want.

I think those are the main points I wanted to cover so I hope the review helps any other curious English speakers!

Yog-Sothoth’s Yard, developed by Bone Nail and published with Shochiku in Japan, is a curious blend of management simulation, strategy, and narrative-driven gameplay wrapped in a setting that draws from both gothic fantasy and Lovecraftian influence. The premise places the player in charge of an old mansion burdened with debts and strange secrets, where the goal is to turn it into a functioning hotel while dealing with otherworldly visitors, staff with supernatural origins, and the constant shadow of ancient forces. At its core, the game challenges players not only to balance resources but also to manage relationships, make narrative decisions, and navigate the thin line between sanity and ambition.

The structure of Yog-Sothoth’s Yard is built around two major pillars: management systems and branching narrative. As the mansion’s new master, you spend your days upgrading rooms, gathering resources, employing staff, and accommodating a variety of guests who bring with them unusual needs and hidden consequences. Action points regulate the pace of the game, and sanity is another crucial factor, particularly when consulting oracles that provide valuable insight at the cost of your mental stability. This tension between short-term gain and long-term risk underpins much of the experience, forcing you to constantly weigh how far to push before resting or recalibrating.

Alchemy and crafting add another dimension to the simulation. Materials harvested from mining or exploration can be combined to create higher-tier items, which in turn feed into room upgrades, hotel services, and even narrative triggers. These mechanics give the player flexibility in how to approach problems: you might focus heavily on refining powerful items, invest in building a luxurious environment to attract certain guests, or pour resources into strengthening staff members to improve survival during difficult events. This variety helps keep the core loop engaging, though repetition in resource gathering can set in during longer sessions.

The cast of characters is one of the most memorable aspects of the game. Staff members such as a dragon alchemist, a grim personification of Death, and a synthetic bioroid maid are not only functional units but also individuals with their own arcs and motivations. Choices you make can strengthen bonds with them, shift the balance of relationships, or open entirely new narrative branches. With over twenty possible endings, the game encourages replayability and experimentation, as each run can unfold in dramatically different ways depending on the paths you follow and the alliances you nurture.

Atmosphere plays a large role in the game’s appeal. The visual style captures both a cozy and unsettling tone, mixing the charm of a management sim with the darker edges of cosmic horror. The manor and its surrounding environments are rendered with enough detail to feel immersive, while the character designs lean into a stylized approach that emphasizes their otherworldly traits. Music and sound are supportive rather than dominant, creating a background mood that shifts as tension rises or quiet moments of management play out. Where the presentation falters is in translation—dialogue can be awkward or confusing due to localization issues, which occasionally undercut the immersion and emotional weight of the story.

Despite its ambitious systems, the game is not without shortcomings. Certain tasks become repetitive, particularly resource collection and room upgrades, which can make the pacing uneven. Some players may find that narrative threads raised in the early stages do not always resolve in satisfying ways, leaving the impression of missed potential. The complexity of systems, while appealing for those who enjoy micromanagement, can feel overwhelming to newcomers, and without careful balance, it is easy to stumble into punishing states where recovery feels difficult. Yet for many, these challenges are part of the game’s charm, adding stakes and unpredictability to every playthrough.

Reception has been generally strong, with a majority of players praising the originality of its design and the way it combines genres that rarely overlap. Its multiple endings, rich atmosphere, and thematic ambition have kept it in positive standing, even as criticisms highlight the grind-heavy aspects and inconsistent localization. For fans of simulation games that thrive on experimentation, or for players who enjoy branching visual novels laced with strategy and occult mystery, it stands out as a distinctive entry that offers hours of replayable content.

In the end, Yog-Sothoth’s Yard succeeds as both a management sim and a narrative experiment. It immerses players in a world that is equal parts eerie and enchanting, where every decision carries weight and no run plays out exactly the same. While its flaws in polish and translation can be distracting, its depth of systems, memorable cast, and atmospheric design more than compensate. For those willing to embrace its quirks, it provides a unique journey through the strange corridors of a haunted mansion where survival, sanity, and success are always delicately intertwined.

Yog-Sothoth's Yard is a game that combines the unlikely elements of hotel management, Lovecraftian lore, and dating simulation. As the inheritor of a mysterious villa laden with shadowy debts, you'll dive headfirst into a world teeming with supernatural beings and enigmatic guests. The premise is intriguing and unique, and it promises a rich gaming experience. However, while it offers a fresh take on the management sim genre, it's not without its share of both positives and negatives.

[h1][b][2] Game Experience : [/b][/h1]

One of the game's standout features is its art direction. The visuals are consistently high-quality, with memorable character designs that add depth to the Lovecraftian atmosphere. The dark and mysterious aesthetic immerses players in a unique world, making it an attractive choice for those who appreciate this kind of art style.

Yog-Sothoth's Yard presents players with a plethora of game mechanics and systems to master. From managing a hotel and upgrading rooms to exploring forests for ingredients and experimenting with alchemy, there's no shortage of activities to keep you engaged. This level of complexity can be a plus for players who enjoy multitasking, but it might overwhelm those looking for a more straightforward gaming experience.

On the downside, the game's English translation leaves much to be desired. While it's serviceable and doesn't render the game incomprehensible, it suffers from inconsistent terminology, typos, and occasional untranslated labels. The story's depth may be appreciated, but the translation may deter some players from fully enjoying it.

The game's narrative, a blend of Lovecraftian horror and dating simulation, offers a unique and engaging premise. However, it falls into the pitfall of becoming somewhat generic and harem-like in its character interactions, which may not appeal to everyone. Additionally, the pacing of the game's story might not meet everyone's expectations, with early intrigue giving way to more stereotypical anime scenes.

[h1][b][3] Verdict : [/b][/h1]

In conclusion, Yog-Sothoth's Yard is a fascinating and innovative game that's worth a try if you appreciate Chinese visual novels, Lovecraftian worlds, and management sims with a twist. OK now for a better desc than this store page gives, you're inheriting some land by your professor/step-father who ran something called "Carnival" where a bunch of enigmatic mask wearing rich ""people"" buy occult/eldritch items auction style, and because you can't sell the land due to the fine print of the inheritance but still need to pay off student debt, you decide to run a hotel as well as fulfill your new obligation to help host Carnival. I grabbed this game absentmindedly, thinking "yeah what the hell, a hotel management dating sim, seems interesting enough." I had no idea what I was in for. This game is pretty fabulous, and I am really hoping it receives more updates over time just to polish things where necessary.  I basically sat down and played it for 13 hours straight and didnt even get halfway through the game yet, because I was exploring so much. 

Visuals: For starters, you open up the game and the first thing you notice is the design. The backgrounds and character designs are all extremely pretty, very well drawn, with a sort of painted art style. It feels like you waltzed into a fairy tale world at first, before you gradually see things get more messed up. The art style is very sleek, and can be quite detailed. It follows a pretty cute chibi style for the overworld, and a more glossy and natural looking backdrop for cutscenes, with intricate backgrounds and visually appealing character designs. No two designs really overlap too much, and everyone has a rather strong stage presence. As your sanity drops and you get farther into the eldritch and occult, there are a few cliche visuals like eyes appearing and tentacles and so on, that have a nice atmosphere for the environment. However, overall the game does a fantastic job at understanding what makes cosmic horror work: tell, dont show. It is the opposite of normal media, but because the horror in this genre comes from the unknowable, showing the effects on people but not elaborating on what caused them visually leaves a lot to the imagination, and the descriptions are perfectly lovecraftian.

Story: The very first part of the VN is a bit tedious, there are no real meaningful choices until you sit through a long prologue, but the prologue sets the scene and stakes very well. You feel rushed the entire time even though it meanders through the auction, as the stakes are front loaded. The characters, including the villains, are all extremely likable as well, and some of their story arcs actually prod on some interesting questions about things like whether or not you can place the value of one life over another and so on. After from this prologue though, the game's story is great. It has a lot of mysteries that you can unravel over the course of the plot, the stakes consistently change, sometimes giving you a break but often taking you on twists and turns. And considering that [spoiler]your memories can and will be tampered with[/spoiler], you are likely to be fully engaged even in the moments where you have few choices.

Heroines: They are all cute, and all of them have distinct personalities. You came here for this, and yes, they are all attractive in their own charming ways, as well as weird and mentally deficient. Oh who is my little psychopath? Yes you are, yes you are.

Dialogue: One of the shortcomings of the game at times. While the writing is overall pretty good, and the language used is very evocative, there are many times where mistranslations or typos took me out of the game for a bit and made me laugh. If you are not too worried about the details, the worst this will do is give you a chuckle here or there at something that is clearly not translated quite right. However the basic writing itself is good, the dialogue with heroines and NPCs is nice, and the quests dont really overstay their welcome. 

Gameplay: The difficulty of this game heavily depends on how you choose to organize your hotel. If you just spam multiplicity, get the extra item that reduces slaughter penalties, and farm guests, then the game can be broken pretty quickly and you will never want for sanity, cleanliness, or money again. Only downside is you have to deal with karmic penalties which may lock some content from you in that run. However, while the gameplay can be repetitive and confusing at times, it is pretty in-depth with a lot of options, so you at least never feel like there is nothing to do. If you struggle with countdowns like me, just remember there are a metric bumload of days in a single playthrough and you have several pages of save slots, so you will be fine. Plan to be a festering cabbage at auctions, those extra items are great to have

[h3] If you are looking for a good Lovecraftian themed visual novel, this is an easy recommend [/h3]
I think generally speaking this game is pretty well made for an indie game and the story is definitely the most rewarding part of the game. However, the game is too much visual novel and not enough of the actual "hotel management/simulation" for me. The idea of an Lovecraftian hotel management sim is interesting and sounds fun, but this idea is unrealized as the player does not have really meaningful interaction with the hotel management mechanics other than collecting supplies and upgrading the rooms to house different Lovecraftian themed guests that provide different resources. The other mini-game that the players interact with is also lacking, alchemy and cooking is find the ingredients and combine them following a set of rules to get what you want, mining is minesweeper, and exploring is click a button and wait until they come back. These mechanics get boring really fast but due to it being a central part of progression within the game it also gets to the point that it can get annoying to interact with these mechanic. These mechanics are also frustrating due to it incorporating RNG, and generally unless there is a point to the RNG (the only point being micro transaction milking my money in gachas) I would not recommend games to incorporate them.

Then there is the story. The overall beats of the story is on point, it is enjoyable, humorous, emotional, and intriguing. Almost all of the characters within the game are well-crafted and like-able, and the Lovecraftian theming is consistent. The plot feels a bit rushed at the end, unless I am missing something the dragon-heart encounter feels a bit out of nowhere. However, the real issue I have with the story is the squandered potential of a Lovecraftian story. The story is a Lovecraftian themed dating sim, not an actual Lovecratian story. It tries to instill the fear of the unknown but utterly fails at that due to it being a dating sim story themed with Cthulhu and Lovecraftian horrors rather than an actual Lovecraftian story. If you are looking for a horror story, there isn't much here. The chapters where it starts to delve into horror ends as quickly as it began, and the horror elements are not strong enough to make it scary. This lightheartedness maybe by design but I truly do think that a real horror story with more mystery is going to be better, however I don't dislike the current story, but it could be better, it could be more Lovecraftian.

As an indie visual novel game, I think it deserves an [b] 8.5~9/10 [/b], however if you come looking for a hotel simulation/management game i think I can only give it around a 7 or a 7.5. But for the price I think this is a steal.

P.S.
Currently from what I can gather, there is a fundraiser for the next game and it seems to be going well. I would love to see the actual hotel simulation part of the game be expanded upon, and upgrade the other game mechanics to more complex and immersive mechanics. I think actually building you hotel would be interesting, something like "tiny towers" but anime and lovecraft could be really good. But yeah, I hope nothing but the best for the developers.

While my experience is overall positive, I have mixed feelings about this visual novel.

First and foremost, I must say that I really enjoyed this game and would definitely recommend it, both for the hotel management mechanics and the narrative surrounding them. Although the introduction was considerably slow and confusing, once you get the gist of how the hotel works, things start to spice up. Through the Oracle and Extra-Objects, you obtain a series of buffs that allow you to speed up your progress and grow your daily revenue. One might feel overwhelmed by the variety of sources available to increase your wealth and the need to organize daily actions efficiently, but the anxiety is minimal compared to its fun.

The art of this game is gorgeous. The Lovecraftian and gloomy atmosphere is perfectly achieved, and each small and cute detail, whether in the environment or in the character designs, create a comfy atmosphere throughout the gameplay. The use of generative AI is present in almost every background of the game and I suspect that in some characters or NPCs too, and while personally I do not mind, others might want to be aware of this before buying it.

The aforementioned characters are the face of the game and the other main point of interest aside from the protagonist’s storyline. Each of them has a unique and interesting story to tell, with their own backgrounds, aspirations, and hopes for the future. Accompanied by a very original and endearing appearance and personality, you will surely fall for at least one of them (Haa Lou Ling, my queen). There are also some great musical pieces scattered here and there. Even though it wasn’t the case for me, the use of a single track during the 48 weeks of the hotel screen might become fairly repetitive and simplistic for some players.

However, and here lies my main issue with the game, the appealing build-up for the characters and events is disappointingly delivered in the later stages. As the weeks go by, the narrative thickens and splits into various subplots between the main cast and the greater mystery surrounding your adoptive father, the destiny of the hotel and the yard, and the outcome of the universe and creations itself. While the player feels deeply engaged and eager to uncover what lies beneath these layers of mystery, their resolution feels rather unsatisfying. Perhaps it's due to the laid-back nature of the life on a hill managing a hotel full of cute girls in the middle of nowhere, but the multiple narrative threads converge artificially from my point of view, not because the story organically leads there, but because they need to be resolved for the main plot to advance. Spontaneous events arise out of nowhere, and with lots of pompous dialogue and cryptic explanations, everything is somehow solved. I didn’t feel that most of the intriguing and mysterious questions raised throughout the game had satisfying resolutions. In an effort to maintain the eerie vibe and fear of the unknown that the game constantly portrays, it fails to follow an organized and enjoyable narrative pace, often overwhelming the player with a barrage of dialogues and events lacking a strong, cohesive thread. It feels as though the main narrative had to move forward no matter what, and although I enjoyed and rushed through the first 70–80% of the game, loving every single bit, the remaining 20% was, to put it mildly, hard to digest.

Finally, the presence of multiple endings is very welcome, offering many possible resolutions for the game and the main character’s fate with their chosen waifu. However, as mentioned before with the main plot, these endings suffer from their own issues. Many, if not almost all, of the endings are unexpectedly brief, leaving the consequences of your choices more to the reader's imagination than actually depicted in-game. For bad endings, this might be seen as a comical or satirical device and can be overlooked, but in the case of your romantic companions, this is inexcusable. Given that these characters accompany and support you from beginning to end, sometimes even willing to sacrifice themselves for their beloved Boss, the main character’s occasionally cold or trying-too-hard-to-look-cool attitude feels unreasonable. One would expect a decent explanation of what happens in the future when you choose character A over B, along with some insight into the fate of the rest of the crew in that timeline. Of course, that’s not the case. The endings are just a few lines long, leaving the rest to daydreams and speculation, which feels rather unfair.

Samely, and following the trend of many visual novels originating from China, the English translation contains several minor grammatical errors and quite a bit of misplaced text. Honestly, this is not a big deal, and the game can be perfectly enjoyed despite these small issues.

In conclusion, let my problems with the final stages of the game not distract you from the overall value and quality of the experience. It is a very entertaining product worth trying, and I praise its creators for the interesting ideas and good intentions poured into this game, even if some parts didn’t meet my expectations. 8.5/10

Having now actually finished the game, I will state bluntly that I straight up loved this experience. To make it brief, the story is far more captivating than the gameplay, the characters are fun and has wonderful personality, and the art (especially character design) are phenomenal. I will be honest to you that the art is what sold me entirely when I first saw this game on steam. So glad to have taken the time to purchase this, and see it all the way through. 

Gameplay:
The game revolves around a hotel management mechanic. It is highly straightforward, and the systems themselves are very simple. Do not expect much complex design and mechanics. If anything, once you got yourself sorted out and know what to do, skipping the gameplay entirely to experience the rest of the story is a very viable option. I would say that gameplay itself should not be the thing that you should focus on at all when you are playing this. 

Story:
Presented in a visual novel format and it is highly captivating. It is very slow at the start because it needs to establish the characters and exposition, but once it picks up it really takes you for a spin. I looked forward to the visual novel experience of Yog-Sothoth Yard very much, because getting to see the characters interact and have fun is something I live for. The atmosphere at the start is very cozy and warm. Super sweet stuff that spikes insulin production in my body. Take your time with learning about the characters in this game because they I would argue are the highlight of this experience

From playing the game, it is already very clear that the game borrows a lot of ideas and elements from Lovecraftian mythos. I myself have not read anything relating to Lovecraft's literature, so it was a big learning experience for me as I sunk the hours into this game. I would say that you don't need to know anything, but looking stuff up now and then really puts things into context. I learned a lot about the books from the little searching I did, and now I am really interested in reading them and learning more. In short, the game kinda acts as a springboard for some other really interesting fiction. Bear with some of the elements you do not understand when you play, because from my own understanding that is entirely the point of Lovecraftian fiction. To not know anything of the truth is a step forward towards comprehending the futility of it all.

Translation:
This is a bit tricky to grapple. The game is an indie product from China, and you should know that translating from Mandarin to English is super finicky. Regardless of that, it is still very readable. I do not speak nor read Mandarin, but I was still able to get the gist of the English translation. You do yourself immense favors by interpreting the actual meaning of what is being stated rather than focusing on the translated definition. Get a feel for the vibe rather than the spoken dialogue really aids a lot in understanding the experience.

Overall, I am happy that I got to play this game. An eye-opening experience for me indeed. If you are interested, come in with an open mind. Do not focus too much on the actual hotel management gameplay, focus more on the story at hand, but more importantly the characters as they breathe life into this package. This is an 11/10 experience and I look forward to what else this studio will cook.
